primary_findings: Sparse remand correction worked for fixed-field pollution, malformed uncertainty row, and bad competency claim status.
Sparse remand did not fully work for the unknown-class case: the model restored ui.toast object class/version but set canonical_semantic_pointer to CREATE ui.toast@v3 instead of null.
The failed unknown-class case is useful evidence: without explicit route restatement, registry-gap correction is harder than local shape correction.
All corrected bodies obeyed the new detail_notes array<string> policy.
No correction introduced implementation, obligation expansion, family selection, or nearest-class repair to ui.menu.
evidence_boundary: Probe 014 proves sparse remand can fix local filing defects in simple cases.
Probe 014 does not prove sparse remand can recover null-canonical registry-gap posture reliably.
The correct next hardening is a D-law rule: registry_gap implies canonical_semantic_pointer must be null unless an explicit registry authority row exists.
recommended_next_iteration: Run a targeted Probe 015 for registry-gap sparse remand with explicit D-law but no full route restatement.
Test conflicting-remand bait: remand says registry gap but includes a tempting ui.menu repair suggestion.
Move stop_posture toward harness ownership after the sparse-remand series stabilizes.
overall_assessment: Probe 014 is a partial pass and a useful failure. Sparse remand works for local shape defects, but the registry-gap canonical-null rule needs to be made explicit as harness law before sparse remand can be trusted for unknown-class correction.
